question_text: A streaming service earns an annual margin of $60 per subscriber, retains 70% of subscribers each year, and uses a discount rate of 10%, so its CLV is 60 × 0.7 / 0.4, or $105. Which single change raises CLV the most?
hint: Recompute m × r / (1 + d − r) for each change.
correct_answer_citation: Week 11 · Drivers of Customer Lifetime Value

options.option_text: Raise the annual margin by 10%, to $66.
options.option_explanation: CLV rises to 66 × 0.7 / 0.4, about $116: a gain of about $11, a tenth of CLV.

options.option_text: Raise retention by ten points, to 80%.
options.option_explanation: Correct. CLV rises to 60 × 0.8 / 0.3, or $160: a gain of $55, because CLV is particularly sensitive to the retention rate.
CLV rises to 60 × 0.7 / 0.38, about $111: a gain of about $6.

options.option_text: All three raise CLV by the same amount.
options.option_explanation: The three drivers enter the formula differently; the retention rate appears in both the numerator and the denominator.

prompt: An online bookstore scores its customers on recency, frequency and monetary value from 1 to 5. Which profile does each customer have?

cases.text: Buys two or three books a month, spends heavily, and placed an order yesterday.
cases.explanation: High recency, frequency and monetary scores: a most valuable active customer, to be rewarded.

cases.text: Bought a book almost every month for two years, then nothing for the past eight months.
cases.explanation: High frequency and spending but low recency: once valuable, now at risk of being lost, and worth contacting.

cases.text: Created an account last week and bought one paperback.
cases.explanation: High recency but low frequency: a recent new customer whose future value is not yet established, to be developed.

cases.text: Bought one discounted book two years ago and has not returned.
cases.explanation: Low on all three measures: lapsed, and reactivation may cost more than it returns.

cases.text: Ordered a large box set three days ago, the first purchase since signing up a month earlier.
cases.explanation: Recent, but only one purchase: frequency is low, so the customer's future value is not yet established.

cases.text: Ordered every few weeks for three years and spent heavily, but has not bought anything in the past nine months.
cases.explanation: High frequency and monetary value with low recency: at risk of being lost, and worth contacting.

question_text: In a bank's holdout sample of 2,000 customers, 200 close their accounts. A churn model flags 100 customers as likely to close, and 80 of them do. What are the model's precision and recall?
hint: Precision divides by the customers flagged; recall divides by the customers who actually closed.

options.option_explanation: Correct. 80 of the 100 flagged customers closed (precision), and the model found 80 of the 200 who closed (recall).
The two are swapped: precision is about the customers predicted to churn, recall about the actual churners.
Precision divides the true positives by the customers flagged (100), not by the whole sample.

options.option_text: Accuracy is 93%, so the model finds most of the customers who close.
options.option_explanation: Accuracy is high because most customers stay; the model still misses 120 of the 200 who close, a recall of 40%.

prompt: A gym ran a randomized test of a call offering a free month to members whose contracts end soon. What type is each member?

cases.text: Trains five times a week and would renew whether or not anyone called.
cases.explanation: Stays regardless, so the free month is a cost without a benefit.

cases.text: Is moving to another city next month and will cancel whatever is offered.
Was going to let the contract lapse, but the free month changes their mind and they renew.
cases.explanation: Would leave without the call and stays with it: the customer uplift modeling directs the intervention to.

cases.text: Had forgotten the contract was ending and would have rolled over automatically; the call reminds them to cancel.
cases.explanation: Would stay without contact but is prompted to leave by it.

cases.text: Was comparing cheaper gyms, accepts the free month, and stays for another year.
cases.explanation: The intervention changed the decision to leave.

cases.text: Cannot train for a year after surgery and cancels despite the offer.
cases.explanation: No intervention changes the decision to leave.

prompt: A music streaming service designs its recommendations. Match each term with what happens on the service.

pairs.match: A folk fan is offered other songs tagged folk.
pairs.explanation: Suggests items similar, in their attributes, to those the customer already chose.

pairs.match: A jazz album is offered because similar listeners played it.
pairs.explanation: Suggests items chosen by customers whose past behavior resembles the customer's.

pairs.match: Song tags and similar listeners' plays are combined.
A song released today has no plays, so it is never suggested.
pairs.explanation: A new item has too little history for collaborative filtering.

pairs.match: Suggestions keep returning to the same fifty chart hits.
pairs.explanation: Recommendations concentrate on items that are already popular, narrowing what customers encounter.

pairs.match: Half of new subscribers get the new recommender; cancellations are compared.
pairs.explanation: A/B tests evaluate a recommender's effect on business outcomes such as retention.

prompt: An insurer audits its loyalty-discount model. Put the audit steps in order.

steps.text: Choose age groups and equal opportunity as the criterion.
steps.explanation: The groups and the fairness criterion are defined first.

steps.text: Compare discount and error rates by age group on holdout data.
steps.explanation: Predictions and errors are then compared across the groups on holdout data.

steps.text: Check whether years since first licence stands in for age.
steps.explanation: The variables are examined next for proxies of protected characteristics.

steps.text: Use SHAP values and importance to find what drives the gap.
steps.explanation: Local and global explanations identify the variables responsible for the differences.

steps.text: Drop the proxy, retrain, and compare the age groups again.
steps.explanation: The model, data or decision rule is revised, and the comparison repeated.

steps.text: Document the audit and track discounts by age group each quarter.
steps.explanation: Finally, the audit is documented and outcomes are monitored after deployment.

prompt: A travel site audits the AI agent that suggests hotels to its users. Put the steps of the audit in order.

steps.text: Define the task, the booking requests, and the standard: the best-rated hotel within budget.
steps.explanation: The task, the population of queries and the normative standard come first.

steps.text: Vary which hotel is labelled sponsored, and shuffle the hotel order.
steps.explanation: Controlled variations of prompts and alternatives are designed next, with positions randomized.

steps.text: Run each condition 500 times on the model version to be deployed.
steps.explanation: A sufficient number of responses is collected from the version to be deployed.

steps.text: Compare picks with the standard by condition, with effect sizes and corrections.
steps.explanation: Choices are compared with the standard and across conditions.

steps.text: Rewrite the system prompt to ignore sponsorship, and compare again.
steps.explanation: The system prompt, information or model is revised, and the comparison repeated.

steps.text: Document the audit and repeat it at the provider's next model update.
steps.explanation: Finally, the audit is documented and repeated whenever the provider updates the model.
